verdict_framing.but_communicate_as: incomplete delivery against the description, NOT defective implementation
verdict_framing.why: Six of ten description bullets are wholly or partly unimplemented. 'Defective' routes to a bug-fix cycle (reproduce, fix, re-verify); 'incomplete' routes back to the story's own scope — to the PM and designer, and to whether this story was finishable as written. A bug-shaped comment sends a scope conversation to the wrong people. The token stays FAIL because nothing downstream recognises a new one, and inventing one breaks the gate math and the release-note refusal logic.
verdict_framing.root_cause: The Story reached READY FOR TEST with its acceptance-criteria field reading '1. No requirements.' That is the mechanism that let six of ten described behaviours go unbuilt with nobody noticing — there was no artifact anyone could check done against. Everything downstream inherited it: 1d had to derive 74 conditions from prose, the verdict is scoped to a spec the ticket does not contain, and the checklist carries a disclaimer saying so. No amount of testing downstream fixes that.

correction_to_a_peer_claim.claim: 'Restore products is in-memory only — so a reload permanently loses the comparison.'
correction_to_a_peer_claim.correction: The first half is right and the conclusion is wrong. The restore BUFFER is in-memory (lastRemovedEntries is a bare ref, cleared on unmount), but the compare LIST itself lives in localStorage and survives a reload — my CMP-027 verified exactly that (reload after Clear all does not resurrect the list, and a populated list persists). What a reload loses is the ability to UNDO a clear, not the comparison. Filing it as 'a reload loses the comparison' would overstate it into a data-loss defect it is not.
